leo-1-the-plan: Page one of five. Meet Leo, a made-up trader with a made-up five thousand dollar account. Before he clicks anything, he writes a plan. Buy at one hundred. Stop at ninety eight. Target at one hundred four.

If the stop is hit, he loses two dollars a share. Any trade can lose. He wrote it before the trade, not after. Tomorrow's page: how many shares is that? That's today's page from my notes. See you tomorrow. — James
leo-2-the-size: Page two of five. Leo, our made-up trader, decides his risk before anything else. One percent of five thousand dollars is fifty dollars. Each share risks two dollars. So fifty divided by two is twenty five shares.

The one percent isn't magic, and any amount can be lost. The point is the loss was chosen in advance. Tomorrow's page: the price goes the wrong way. That's today's page from my notes. See you tomorrow. — James
leo-3-the-stop: Page three of five. Leo bought twenty five shares at one hundred, and the price starts to slip. Ninety nine. Then ninety eight. Part of him wants to move the stop lower. His plan says no.

The stop is hit. He loses fifty dollars, exactly what he planned. His made-up account is now four thousand nine hundred fifty. Tomorrow's page: what Leo writes down. That's today's page from my notes. See you tomorrow. — James
leo-4-the-journal: Page four of five. That evening, Leo writes his journal entry. Was the plan followed? Yes. Result? Minus fifty dollars. Feeling at exit? Annoyed. He notes that following the plan and losing can both be true.

A loss that follows the plan isn't a mistake. It's part of trading. The journal keeps those two things apart. Tomorrow's page: the one rule Leo changes. That's today's page from my notes. See you tomorrow. — James
leo-5-the-rule: Page five of five. Reading his notes, Leo spots a pattern. The urge to trade again came within minutes of the stop. So he adds one rule. After any stop, wait fifteen minutes before looking for another trade.
He will check that rule against his journal next week. It might help, or it might not. Trading carries a real risk of loss. That's today's page from my notes. See you tomorrow. — James
